extraction.name: LAMBADA
extraction.description: LAMBADA (LAnguage Modeling Broadened to Account for Discourse Aspects) is a word-prediction benchmark comprising 10,022 narrative passages: 4,869 development passages and 5,153 test passages. Human subjects can predict each passage's final word given the whole passage, but not given only the final sentence. A separate training corpus contains 2,662 novels comprising 203 million words.
extraction.creator: Denis Papemo; Germán Kruszewski; Angeliki Lazaridou; Quan Ngoc Pham; Raffaella Bemardi; Sandro Pezzelle; Marco Baroni; Gemma Boleda; Raquel Femández
extraction.citeAs: Denis Papemo, Germán Kruszewski, Angeliki Lazaridou, Quan Ngoc Pham, Raffaella Bemardi, Sandro Pezzelle, Marco Baroni, Gemma Boleda, and Raquel Femández. 2016. The LAMBADA dataset: Word prediction requiring a broad discourse context. Proceedings of the 54th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, pages 1525–1534, Berlin, Germany, August 7–12.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Passages were extracted from the Book Corpus. Each passage contains a target sentence and the minimum number of preceding complete sentences needed to supply at least 50 context tokens. Novels were randomly partitioned into training and development/testing groups, with development and test novels also kept disjoint. Four language models filtered out passages with relatively predictable final words. A random sample of remaining passages underwent three-stage crowdsourced screening: two consecutive subjects had to predict the original final word from the whole passage, while subjects shown only the target sentence had to fail to predict it. More than 200,000 passages were presented at the first human-screening stage; approximately one in 25 input examples passed all selection steps.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The source was the Book Corpus (Zhu et al., 2015), containing unpublished novels. After duplicate removal and filtering potentially offensive material, the source corpus contained 5,325 novels and 465 million words.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Novels were randomly divided into approximately equal training and development/testing partitions. Development and test passages were subsequently separated by novel, yielding 4,869 development passages from 1,331 novels and 5,153 test passages from 1,332 novels. The prediction target is the original final word of the target sentence, which is withheld for the word-completion task.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Duplicate novels were removed, and potentially offensive material was filtered using a stop-word list. Passage context was constructed from the minimum number of complete preceding sentences containing at least 50 tokens. Passages were excluded if their target word had probability at least 0.00175 under any of four language models: a pretrained recurrent neural network, and a standard 4-gram model, recurrent neural network, and feed-forward model trained on the Book Corpus. Human screening then retained only passages whose target words were predictable with broad context but not with sentence-only context.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Through CrowdFlower, a first subject guessed the final word from the whole passage. If correct, a second subject independently guessed it from the whole passage. If both were correct, additional subjects attempted prediction from the target sentence alone, until the word was guessed or ten unsuccessful judgments were reached. Sentence-only subjects could provide three guesses per sentence. A passage was retained only if both whole-passage subjects exactly matched the original word and none of the ten sentence-only subjects guessed it. The same subject could not judge the same item in both conditions. Whole-passage tasks paid $0.22 per page of ten passages; sentence-only tasks paid $0.15 per page of twenty sentences.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Selection used a strict exact-match, hit-or-miss criterion rather than accepting plausible or synonymous continuations. A pilot study showed that one successful whole-passage guess did not reliably establish that a passage was easy with broad context, so a second successful whole-passage judgment was required. Approximately 84–86% of items were discarded at stage 1, an additional 6–7% at stage 2, and another 3–5% at stage 3. Evaluating alternative acceptable answers through additional human raters was considered financially and practically infeasible.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: For each retained passage, two successful whole-passage judgments and ten unsuccessful sentence-only judgments; sentence-only subjects were allowed three guesses each.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The development set and training corpus were available for download at the dataset website. The authors planned a public competition and stated that the test set would be made available at the time of that competition.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: More than 80% of passages contain the target word in their context, compared with less than 15% of the input sample. Proper nouns constitute 48% of targets and are substantially overrepresented relative to the input; common nouns constitute 37%, and verbs 7.7%. Pronouns constitute only 0.3%. The sentence-final target position skews the input toward nouns, and human filtering further favors nouns over other parts of speech. Quoted direct speech occurs in 71% of LAMBADA passages versus 61% of the input sample. The single-word completion constraint excludes multiword referring expressions. Filtering explicitly selects passages on which standard language models struggle.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: LAMBADA evaluates specially selected, harder-than-average passages rather than average language-modeling cases. Its exact-match criterion excludes plausible or synonymous alternative continuations. Cost constraints limited the number of whole-passage judgments and prevented additional ratings of alternative answers. The training corpus is from the same domain but is not filtered like the development and test passages. The authors intend the benchmark to evaluate general-purpose broad-context understanding, not to support ad-hoc models designed only for its particular passage format. A small apparent proportion of proper-noun targets absent from context was attributed to lemmatization errors; manual checking confirmed that all proper-noun targets occurred in context.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Evaluate general-purpose language models and computational text-understanding systems through final-word prediction requiring broad discourse context. Train language models on the separate raw-text training partition, use development data for tuning or fine-tuning, and evaluate on the held-out test passages. The principal evaluation measure is target-word prediction accuracy. The authors recommend training on general unsupervised word prediction rather than only tailoring models to LAMBADA-style examples, and emphasize that models should handle ordinary language-modeling cases as well as difficult broad-context cases.
